ak_sky_pilot.blurb: Sky Pilot is a small wall right beside the Seward Highway south of Anchorage, close to sea level. It holds a varied mix: trad lines are the biggest group, followed by boulder problems, a few sport routes and two aid climbs. Free routes bunch up around 5.10, with a handful of hard 5.12 and 5.13 lines and a single 5.9 for contrast. The boulder problems run mostly V2 to V3, with one far harder outlier. Some of the routes have been reported as deteriorating or partly collapsed, so this suits experienced parties who judge hold and bolt condition on the spot, not first-timers looking for a mellow day.
ak_sky_pilot.parking_note: Pull off the highway directly in front of the wall, a little over 5 miles south of the weigh station near mile marker 109.4.

ak_lost_world_middle_earth.blurb: This is a talus boulderfield in Archangel Valley at Hatcher Pass, sitting just south of the Diamond South talus and short of Sydney Creek Bowl. Seventeen problems are recorded here, all bouldering, on granite. The spread is wide: a good number of easy problems from V0 to V2, a middle group around V3 to V5, and a pair of tough lines at V8, so both newer and strong boulderers have something. Locals have split on its name, calling it either Lost World or Middle Earth. Expect a typical alpine boulderfield, with a creek to cross on the way in.

ak_marmot_rock_tr_trad.blurb: Marmot Rock is a sizable formation a short stroll up the east side of the Savage River valley in Denali National Park, near the end of the public road. Climbs are on its north, west and south sides, split almost evenly between top-rope and trad. Most lines are short, some barely taller than a big boulder problem, and grades span from easy fifth class up to a single 5.11, with the bulk in the 5.7 to 5.10 range. Rock quality varies and loose pieces are common, though holds clean up with traffic. Landings can be hard, and hikers share the area, so watch gear and loose rock.

ak_right_cave.blurb: Right Cave is a steep, overhanging cave on the cliff at Weiner Lake, off the Glenn Highway east of Palmer and roughly an hour and a half from Anchorage. It belongs to the one place in Alaska with a real concentration of sport climbing. Nearly all of the seventeen routes are bolted, with just two trad lines, and the grades are firmly in hard territory: a few 5.11s, a large group of 5.12s and 5.13s, and one 5.14. The igneous rock forms big stacked pillars with cracks, pockets, slopers and pinches, and several lines go in two or three pitches. The cave catches sun well into the afternoon. Not a place for beginners.

ak_lower_pivot_point.blurb: Lower Pivot Point is the lower wall of the Pivot Point cliffs beside the Seward Highway south of Anchorage. It packs a lot into a small space: trad is the largest group, with boulder problems, sport routes, top-ropes and one mixed traverse filling out the rest. Free climbs run from 5.7 up through the 5.11s and into the 5.14 range, with a cluster at 5.11, while the boulder problems span a wide range of difficulty. It is easy to scramble to the top and rig top-ropes, which makes it handy for a casual session. Watch for loose holds. The broader Pivot Point area tends to be shady and sheltered from wind.
ak_lower_pivot_point.approach: From the highway, follow the faint trail to a fork and take the right branch up to the large wall.

ak_ravendale_aka_lost_crack.blurb: Ravendale, also known as Lost Crack, is one of the subareas of West Grapefruit Rocks, a limestone outcrop on a low dome in the boreal forest off the Elliott Highway north of Fairbanks. Of its sixteen routes, most are sport, with a couple of trad lines and one top-rope. Grades run from an easy 5.6 through the heart of the range at 5.9 to 5.11, with a few climbs in the 5.12 and 5.13 zone. Expect polished limestone and thin edges, so footwork matters. The setting is airy, and the crag is a reasonable stop for a mixed group wanting moderate to mid-grade sport.

ak_black_lakes_crag.blurb: Black Lakes Crag is a small cliff just above the pair of lakes beside the Klondike Highway north of Skagway, in Southeast Alaska. It offers a mix of bolted lines and trad cracks, with trad making up about two thirds of the sixteen routes. The grades are moderate: mostly 5.9 and 5.10, a few 5.11s, and a couple of easier 5.7 and 5.8 lines. A day here is plenty for most parties. Because the wall sits by the road and the base of most sport routes is a short hike up a hill, logistics are simple, though loose and eroding ground below some lines calls for care.
ak_black_lakes_crag.parking_note: Drive north from Skagway on the Klondike Highway past both lakes and use the large pullout just beyond the second one; the rock is on the hillside across the road.

ak_jaw_man_zone.blurb: Jaw Man Zone is a cliff system on Jaw Point, on the coast about 15 miles south of Juneau, and the first big wall on the north side of the South Gully as you walk uphill. A boat ride is the only way in. Trad dominates the fifteen routes, with a few sport lines and a couple of hard boulder problems. Climbing is technical, sporty and slightly off vertical, with several multipitch lines. Most free routes sit in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, plus one easier option and one 5.12. This is a committed outing for competent parties comfortable with marine travel, not a casual crag.
